title: How synchronized works underneath
context: How does synchronized work at the JVM level?

source.title: JavaGuide (Snailclimb): Java concurrency questions (2 of 3)
source.note: Question and topic from this JavaGuide article. The answer is an original English write-up; see content/sources/javaguide/NOTICE.md.

answer: Every object has a monitor, stored in its header. `synchronized` acquires the monitor on entry and releases it on exit, including when an exception is thrown. A synchronized method locks `this` or the class object for static methods. Since Java 6 the JVM optimises locks: biased locking has been disabled by default since JDK 15, and thin locks use a CAS on the header first, then inflate to a full OS mutex under contention. Only one thread holds a monitor at a time, and the memory rules give visibility.

points.title: Monitor per object
points.why: Every object carries a monitor. synchronized takes it on entry and releases it on exit.

points.title: Visibility
points.why: Releasing a monitor makes the thread's writes visible to the next thread that takes it.

points.title: Lock escalation
points.why: Uncontended locks are cheap. Contention inflates them to OS-level locks.
